blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 12 (Human Skeletal and Muscular Systems), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is a skeleton? Write its functions.
blocks.explanation: Bones, cartilage and other connective tissues make an internal framework called the skeleton. It provides structural support, protects vital organs, and produces movement and locomotion.

book_ref.quote: make an internal framework called skeleton that provides structural support

blocks.prompt: 2 What is periosteum? How is it held to the bone?
blocks.explanation: Periosteum is the tough membrane covering the surface of a bone. Collagen fibres anchor it to the underlying bone tissue, which gives the bone additional strength and stability.

book_ref.quote: Collagen fibres anchor the periosteum to the underlying bone tissue

blocks.prompt: 3 What is a Haversian system? Name its parts.
blocks.explanation: The Haversian system is the basic structural unit of compact bone. Its parts are: lamellae (concentric layers of mineralized matrix), lacunae with osteocytes, canaliculi (small channels), and a central Haversian canal containing blood vessels, nerves and lymphatic vessels.

book_ref.quote: The basic structural units of compact bone are called Haversian systems

blocks.prompt: 4 What are lamellae? What do they contain?
blocks.explanation: Lamellae are concentric layers of mineralized extracellular matrix in a Haversian system. They contain collagen fibres and small, needle-shaped crystals of calcium phosphate.

book_ref.quote: These are concentric layers of mineralized extracellular matrix

blocks.prompt: 5 Give reason: bone is both strong and flexible.
blocks.explanation: The calcium phosphate crystals of the lamellae are brittle but rigid and give bone great strength, while collagen is flexible but weak. Together they make bone both strong and flexible.

book_ref.quote: The crystals are brittle but rigid, giving bone great strength.

blocks.prompt: 6 What are canaliculi? Write their role.
blocks.explanation: Canaliculi are small channels in a Haversian system. They connect the osteocytes (lying in lacunae) to each other and to the Haversian canal.

book_ref.quote: by small channels called canaliculi

blocks.prompt: 7 Differentiate between red bone marrow and yellow bone marrow.
blocks.explanation: Red marrow makes blood cells; yellow marrow is a fat store in the shafts of long bones.

book_ref.quote: Many bones also contain a soft tissue called bone marrow

rows: Found in spongy bone, ends of long bones, ribs, vertebrae, sternum and pelvis
Fills the shafts of long bones
Produces red blood cells, platelets and white blood cells
Consists mostly of fat cells and serves as an energy reserve
Works as the blood-forming tissue
Can be converted to red marrow and produce blood cells when severe blood loss occurs

blocks.prompt: 8 Differentiate between epiphysis and diaphysis.
blocks.explanation: Both are parts of a long bone.

book_ref.quote: the middle part along the length of bone is called diaphysis or shaft

rows: The broad ends of a bone
The middle part along the length of the bone
Lie at the two ends of the bone
Also called the shaft

blocks.prompt: 9 Give reason: bones are not dry, rigid structures.
blocks.explanation: Bones only appear dry and rigid. They are moist, living tissues with living bone cells (osteoblasts, osteocytes, osteoclasts), blood vessels and nerves; despite their number and size they make up less than 20% of the body's mass.

book_ref.quote: They are moist, living tissues.

blocks.prompt: 10 Differentiate between osteoblasts and osteoclasts.
blocks.explanation: One forms bone, the other breaks it down.

book_ref.quote: The work of osteoclasts is important to the growth and repair of bone.

rows: Bone-forming cells
Bone-resorbing cells
Synthesize and secrete unmineralized ground substance
Break down bone and release calcium and phosphate in blood
Become osteocytes when surrounded by matrix
Develop from macrophages

blocks.prompt: 11 What is osteogenesis? Name its two pathways.
blocks.explanation: Osteogenesis is the process of bone formation; it begins in the embryo and continues throughout life. Its two pathways are: (1) formation of long bones (e.g. femur, humerus) from cartilage, and (2) direct development of a few bones (e.g. some skull bones) into hard bone without cartilage.

book_ref.quote: There are two primary pathways of osteogenesis.

blocks.prompt: 12 What is the role of blood vessels in the formation of a long bone?
blocks.explanation: When the centre of the cartilage calcifies and its chondrocytes die, cavities are left. Blood vessels penetrate these cavities and bring in osteoblasts, which build bone tissue, and osteoclasts, which break down calcified cartilage to make room for more bone.

book_ref.quote: Blood vessels penetrate these cavities and introduce osteoblasts and osteoclasts.

blocks.prompt: 13 What is bone remodelling?
blocks.explanation: Even after bones are fully formed, osteogenesis continues as bone remodelling: old bone is broken down by osteoclasts and new bone is formed by osteoblasts.

book_ref.quote: This ongoing process involves the breakdown of old bone by osteoclasts

blocks.prompt: 14 Where does cartilage remain throughout life? Why?
blocks.explanation: Most foetal cartilage is replaced by bone, but some remains throughout life to provide flexibility: at the areas between bones, at the end of the nose, in the outer ear and along the inside of the trachea.

book_ref.quote: some cartilage remains throughout life and provides flexibility

blocks.prompt: 15 What is perichondrium? Write its role.
blocks.explanation: Perichondrium is the layer of connective tissue that surrounds cartilage. It contains blood vessels, lymphatic vessels and nerves that supply the cartilage tissue.

book_ref.quote: It contains blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and nerves that supply the cartilage tissue.

blocks.prompt: 16 Give reason: cartilage heals very slowly.
blocks.explanation: Unlike other connective tissues, there are no blood vessels inside the cartilage matrix. Its cells are supplied only by diffusion, so cartilage heals very slowly.

book_ref.quote: Because of this, it heals very slowly.

blocks.prompt: 17 Differentiate between hyaline cartilage and fibrocartilage.
blocks.explanation: Both are types of cartilage, found in different places.

book_ref.quote: Cartilage can be classified into three types.

rows: The most common type of cartilage
Found where the body experiences high stress and tension
Found in the nose, trachea and articulating surfaces of bones in joints
Found in intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis
Joins the first rib and sternum
Joins bones in the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs

blocks.prompt: 18 Differentiate between bone and cartilage.
blocks.explanation: Both are connective tissues of the skeleton.

book_ref.quote: Has limited ability to repair itself, as it has no direct blood supply

rows: Covered by periosteum
Covered by perichondrium
Cells: osteoblasts, osteocytes and osteoclasts
Cells: chondrocytes
Matrix contains calcium crystals and collagen fibres
Matrix contains collagen and other fibres
Blood vessels present
Blood vessels absent
Can grow and repair itself throughout life
Limited ability to repair itself, as it has no direct blood supply

blocks.prompt: 19 Differentiate between cranial bones and facial bones.
blocks.explanation: Both are bones of the 22-bone skull.

book_ref.quote: Fourteen facial bones are attached to the cranium.

rows: Eight bones
Fourteen bones
Form the cranium (brain box)
Are attached to the cranium
Paired: parietal and temporal
Paired: lacrimal, zygomatic, nasal, inferior nasal concha, maxilla, palatine
Unpaired: frontal, occipital, ethmoid, sphenoid
Unpaired: mandible (jaw bone) and vomer

blocks.prompt: 20 What are ear ossicles? How many are there?
blocks.explanation: Ossicles are the small bones of the middle ear: malleus, incus and stapes. There are 6 ossicles in all (3 pairs), three in each middle ear.

book_ref.quote: There are 6 bones (3 pairs) in middle ears.

blocks.prompt: 21 What is the hyoid bone? Write one special feature of it.
blocks.explanation: The hyoid is the neck bone: a small single bone at the base of the skull below the tongue. Its special feature is that it does not articulate with any other bone of the head.

book_ref.quote: Hyoid bone is a small single bone which lies at the base of skull below the tongue.

blocks.prompt: 22 What is the sacrum? With which bones does it articulate?
blocks.explanation: The sacrum is formed by five fused sacral vertebrae. It articulates with the iliac bones of the hip to form the back of the pelvis.

book_ref.quote: The sacrum articulates with the iliac bones of the hip to form the back of the pelvis.

blocks.prompt: 23 Differentiate between clavicle and scapula.
blocks.explanation: Both are bones of the pectoral girdle, one pair each.

book_ref.quote: One end of each clavicle articulates with the sternum.

rows: Collar bone
Shoulder bone
One end articulates with the sternum, the other with the scapula
Articulates with the clavicle

blocks.prompt: 24 Differentiate between ulna and radius.
blocks.explanation: Both are long bones of the forelimb.

book_ref.quote: Ulna is slightly bigger than radius.

rows: On the inner side of the arm
On the outer side (thumb side)
Slightly bigger
Slightly smaller
Long bone of the forelimb
Long bone; the upper row of carpals articulates with it to form the wrist joint

blocks.prompt: 25 Differentiate between carpals and tarsals.
blocks.explanation: Both are short bones; carpals are in the forelimb, tarsals in the hindlimb. (The book prints 'carpels'; the correct word is carpals.)

book_ref.quote: These are short bones which are tightly attached to form the ankle.

rows: Eight bones
Seven bones
Present in two rows and form the wrist
Tightly attached to form the ankle
Upper row articulates with the radius to form the wrist joint
Articulate with the metatarsals

blocks.prompt: 26 What is the acetabulum? What fits into it?
blocks.explanation: The acetabulum is the bony socket in each hip bone, formed by the fusion of its three bones (ilium, ischium and pubis). The head of the femur fits into it.

book_ref.quote: that is composed of the fusion of three bones

blocks.prompt: 27 What is the pubic symphysis?
blocks.explanation: The pubic symphysis is a cartilaginous joint that joins the two hip bones at the front by connecting the pubic bones at the midline of the body. Its bones are connected by fibrocartilage.

book_ref.quote: a cartilaginous joint that connects the pubic bones at the midline of the body

blocks.prompt: 28 Differentiate between tibia and fibula.
blocks.explanation: Both are bones of the lower leg.

book_ref.quote: Fibula or outer bone is a thin bone that joins the tibia

rows: Shin bone
Outer bone
The large bone in the leg
A thin bone
Main bone of the lower leg
Joins the tibia just below the knee joint and just above the ankle

blocks.prompt: 29 What is the patella? Where is it located?
blocks.explanation: The patella or kneecap is one of the 30 bones of each hindlimb. It is embedded in a long tendon that runs over the knee joint; the quadriceps are inserted on it.

book_ref.quote: It is embedded in a long tendon which runs over the knee joint.

blocks.prompt: 30 What is a joint? Name its three major kinds with their movement.
blocks.explanation: A joint is a place where two bones, or bone and cartilage, come together. Kinds: fibrous joints (immovable), cartilaginous joints (slightly movable) and synovial joints (freely movable).

book_ref.quote: Three major kinds of joints are found in human body

blocks.prompt: 31 What is articular cartilage? Write its function.
blocks.explanation: Articular cartilage is a smooth, tough and elastic hyaline cartilage that covers the ends of the bones in a synovial joint. It provides a smooth and frictionless surface for movement.

book_ref.quote: It provides a smooth and frictionless surface for movement.

blocks.prompt: 32 What is the fibrous capsule of a synovial joint? What is it made of?
blocks.explanation: The fibrous capsule surrounds a synovial joint and helps hold the bones together. It has an outer layer of ligaments and an inner lining of synovial membrane, which secretes synovial fluid that lubricates the joint.

book_ref.quote: A fibrous capsule surrounds the synovial joint and helps to hold the bones together.

blocks.prompt: 33 Differentiate between ball-and-socket joint and hinge joint.
blocks.explanation: Both are synovial joints with different ranges of motion.

book_ref.quote: Ball-and-socket joints allow motion in all directions e.g., shoulder

rows: Allows motion in all directions
Allows movement in only one plane, like a door hinge
Examples: shoulder and hip joints
Examples: elbow and knee joints

blocks.prompt: 34 Differentiate between pivot joint and gliding joint.
blocks.explanation: Both are synovial joints.

book_ref.quote: Gliding joints allow gliding movements between bones

rows: Allows rotational movement around a single axis
Allows gliding movements between bones
Example: joint between the first and second vertebrae of the neck
Examples: joints between the vertebrae and between the bones in wrist and ankle

blocks.prompt: 35 Differentiate between ellipsoidal joint and saddle joint.
blocks.explanation: Both allow movement in two planes.

book_ref.quote: Saddle joints allow movement in two planes because

rows: Allows movement in two planes but not rotation
Allows movement in two planes because one bone has a concave and the other a convex surface
Example: joint of wrist with radius
Example: thumb joint

blocks.prompt: 36 What is joint transplantation?
blocks.explanation: Joint transplantation is a surgical procedure in which a damaged joint is replaced with a healthy natural joint from a donor or with an artificial joint.

book_ref.quote: It is a surgical procedure in which a damaged joint is replaced

blocks.prompt: 37 Differentiate between total joint replacement and partial joint replacement.
blocks.explanation: Both are types of joint transplantation.

book_ref.quote: only the damaged part of the joint is replaced with an artificial component

rows: The entire damaged joint is replaced
Only the damaged part of the joint is replaced
Replaced with an artificial joint made of metal, plastic or ceramic
Replaced with an artificial component
Whole joint is changed
Often used in the knee joint

blocks.prompt: 38 What is chondrocyte implantation?
blocks.explanation: Chondrocyte implantation is a type of joint transplantation in which chondrocytes (cartilage cells) from the patient's own joint are implanted into the damaged joint. It is often used in the knee joint.

book_ref.quote: Chondrocyte implantation: In this procedure

blocks.prompt: 39 How do the human pelvis and buttock muscles help in bipedal posture?
blocks.explanation: The human pelvis is shorter and broader, which stabilizes the torso and supports the body's weight on two legs. The buttock muscles are much larger in humans; they stabilize the torso and propel the body forward while walking.

book_ref.quote: Human pelvis is shorter and broader

blocks.prompt: 40 How do the femur and toes of humans suit walking on two legs?
blocks.explanation: The human femur is angled inward towards the knee joint, keeping the body's centre of mass over the feet for stability while standing and walking. The toes are shorter and less prehensile, so the foot works better as a lever in walking and running.

book_ref.quote: The human femur is also angled inward towards the knee joint

blocks.prompt: 41 Name three problems caused by improper posture.
blocks.explanation: (1) Vertebral misalignment: back and neck pain and herniated discs. (2) Joint strain: pain and inflammation of neck, shoulders, hips and knees, possibly arthritis. (3) Muscle imbalances: overused and underused muscles pull bones and joints out of alignment.

book_ref.quote: Improper posture can negatively affect bones and joints

blocks.prompt: 42 Which parts of the skeletal system can be affected by its disorders?
blocks.explanation: Skeletal disorders can impact the structure and function of any part of the skeletal system, including bones, joints and connective tissues.

book_ref.quote: Skeletal system is susceptible to a wide range of disorders

blocks.prompt: 43 What is the role of intervertebral discs? What can cause a slipped disc?
blocks.explanation: Intervertebral discs between the vertebrae act as shock absorbers and help in movement. A slipped disc may be due to trauma, degenerative changes due to aging, or repetitive strain on the vertebral column.

book_ref.quote: act as shock absorbers and help in movement

blocks.prompt: 44 Differentiate between disc slip and spondylosis.
blocks.explanation: Both are disorders of the vertebral column that can press on nerves or the spinal cord.

book_ref.quote: It may result in narrowing and fusion of intervertebral disc

rows: The outer layer of an intervertebral disc tears and the inner gel-like substance leaks out
Degeneration of vertebrae, intervertebral discs, ligaments or cartilage of the vertebral column
Due to trauma, aging changes or repetitive strain
Mostly natural degeneration of discs with aging; also genetic factors, trauma, poor posture and obesity
Symptoms: pain, numbness, tingling, weakness; severe cases bowel or bladder dysfunction
Symptoms: back or neck pain, stiffness and reduced range of motion

blocks.prompt: 45 Write the causes of spondylosis.
blocks.explanation: The most common cause is the natural degeneration of intervertebral discs. It occurs with aging, genetic factors, trauma, and prolonged periods of poor posture and obesity.

book_ref.quote: The most common cause is the natural degeneration of intervertebral discs.

blocks.prompt: 46 What is the sciatic nerve? Why can a slipped disc cause sciatica?
blocks.explanation: The sciatic nerve starts from the lower back and goes through the buttocks into each leg. A herniated or bulging disc can press on this nerve; this compression or irritation of the sciatic nerve is sciatica.

book_ref.quote: Sciatica means compression or irritation of the sciatic nerve.

blocks.prompt: 47 Differentiate between rheumatoid arthritis and gouty arthritis.
blocks.explanation: Both are types of arthritis (inflammatory joint conditions).

book_ref.quote: Gouty arthritis (or gout) occurs when there is a build-up of uric acid

rows: Result of an autoimmune disorder
Due to build-up of uric acid in the blood
The synovial membrane becomes inflamed
Uric acid forms crystals in the joints and causes inflammation
Most commonly the wrist and hands are involved
Most commonly the joint of the big toe; knees, wrists and fingers may also be affected

blocks.prompt: 48 What is arthritis? Name its common symptoms.
blocks.explanation: Arthritis includes different inflammatory conditions that affect the joints. Symptoms of all types are joint pain and stiffness; others may be redness, warmth and swelling in the affected joints.

book_ref.quote: Symptoms of all types include joint pain and stiffness.

blocks.prompt: 49 What is osteoporosis?
blocks.explanation: Osteoporosis is a condition of weakened bones that are more prone to fractures and breaks. It occurs when bone density decreases, making the bones fragile and porous.

book_ref.quote: It occurs when bone density decreases

blocks.prompt: 50 Why are calcium and vitamin D important for preventing osteoporosis?
blocks.explanation: Calcium is crucial for bone strength, while vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium. A lack of calcium and vitamin D in the diet impairs bone health and is a cause of osteoporosis.

book_ref.quote: Calcium is crucial for bone strength

blocks.prompt: 51 Name two lifestyle factors and one treatment that increase the risk of osteoporosis.
blocks.explanation: Lifestyle factors: lack of weight-bearing exercise; smoking and alcohol consumption. Treatment: long-term use of corticosteroids.

book_ref.quote: Smoking and alcohol consumption can also increase the risk of osteoporosis.

blocks.prompt: 52 Differentiate between dislocation and sprain.
blocks.explanation: Both are common injuries to joints.

book_ref.quote: Joints can be subject to a variety of injuries

rows: Bones in a joint are forced out of their normal positions
Injury to the ligaments that connect bones in a joint
Due to a sudden impact or trauma; rheumatoid arthritis can also cause it
Happens when the joint is forced beyond its normal range of motion
Severe cases tear muscles, ligaments and tendons
Ligaments stretch or tear; commonly in ankle, knee and wrist
Reduced by a doctor; surgery may be needed for stretched ligaments
Usually treated with physical therapy and dressing

blocks.prompt: 53 Write the symptoms of a dislocation.
blocks.explanation: Symptoms of a dislocation are swelling, intense pain and immobility of the affected joint. A severe dislocation can also tear muscles, ligaments and tendons.

book_ref.quote: Symptoms include swelling, intense pain, and immobility of the affected joint.

blocks.prompt: 54 How is a sprain treated?
blocks.explanation: Sprains are usually treated with physical therapy. Dressing is done to immobilize the sprain and provide support.

book_ref.quote: Dressings is done to immobilize the sprain and provide support.

blocks.prompt: 55 Name the first aid steps for a dislocation or sprain.
blocks.explanation: (1) Immobilize the area with a sling or splint; do not try to re-align the joint. (2) Apply an ice pack or cold compress. (3) Elevate the affected limb if possible. (4) Seek medical attention: call 1122 or take the person to hospital.

book_ref.quote: First aid treatment for dislocation and sprain includes the following steps

blocks.prompt: 56 Why are ice and elevation of the limb used in the first aid of a dislocation?
blocks.explanation: An ice pack or cold compress reduces swelling and pain. Elevating the affected limb, if possible, also helps reduce swelling.

book_ref.quote: elevate the affected limb above to help reduce swelling

blocks.prompt: 57 Define muscle. What are muscle fibres?
blocks.explanation: Muscle is the tissue that can contract in a coordinated way to produce movements of body parts or the whole body. The individual cells of muscle are called muscle fibres or myofibres.

book_ref.quote: Muscle is defined as the tissue that can contract

blocks.prompt: 58 Differentiate between skeletal muscle and smooth muscle.
blocks.explanation: Both are muscle tissues of the human body.

book_ref.quote: Skeletal muscles are responsible for moving parts of the body

rows: Moves parts of the body: limbs, trunk and face
In the walls of stomach, intestines, blood vessels and other internal organs
Elongated fibres with regular striations
Spindle-shaped fibres without striations
Many nuclei per cell
One nucleus per cell
Voluntary (usually consciously controlled)
Involuntary (usually no voluntary control)

blocks.prompt: 59 Write the function of each of the three types of muscle tissue.
blocks.explanation: Skeletal muscle: to move the skeleton. Smooth muscle: to move substances through hollow organs. Cardiac muscle: to pump blood.

book_ref.quote: Human body has three types of muscle tissues

blocks.prompt: 60 Give two examples to show that animals other than humans also use muscles.
blocks.explanation: (1) When a mosquito flies, its wings are moved rapidly by quickly contracting flight muscles. (2) When an earthworm burrows through soil, strong muscles push its body past the surrounding soil.

book_ref.quote: when a mosquito flies, its wings are moved rapidly

blocks.prompt: 61 What are T-tubules? Where do they reach?
blocks.explanation: T-tubules (transverse tubules) are hollow elongated tubes formed when the sarcolemma penetrates deep into the muscle fibre. They reach the ends of the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) and carry the impulse inside.

book_ref.quote: The T-tubules reach the ends of SR.

blocks.prompt: 62 Give reason: skeletal muscle looks striped (striated).
blocks.explanation: In myofibrils, thick myosin filaments create dark A-bands and thin actin filaments create light I-bands. These alternating dark and light bands give skeletal muscle its striped appearance.

book_ref.quote: These alternating dark and light bands give skeletal muscle its striped

blocks.prompt: 63 What are Z-lines? Define sarcomere.
blocks.explanation: Z-lines are protein discs to which the thin actin filaments are attached. The section of a myofibril between two Z-lines is a sarcomere, the smallest unit of muscle contraction.

book_ref.quote: The thin actin filaments are attached to protein discs called Z-lines.

blocks.prompt: 64 Summarize the structural organization of a skeletal muscle.
blocks.explanation: A skeletal muscle is made of groups of cells called muscle fibres. Each muscle fibre contains bundles of myofibrils in its cytoplasm. Each myofibril is made of two types of myofilaments, myosin and actin.

book_ref.quote: Each muscle fibre contains bundles of myofibrils in its cytoplasm.

blocks.prompt: 65 Differentiate between thick and thin myofilaments.
blocks.explanation: Both are myofilaments of a myofibril.

book_ref.quote: These myosin heads extend from the thick filaments

rows: About 16 nm in diameter
7-8 nm in diameter
Made of many myosin proteins
Made of actin, tropomyosin and troponin
Myosin heads extend from it and connect to actin
Has myosin binding sites on actin; attached to Z-lines
Creates the dark A-band
Creates the light I-band

blocks.prompt: 66 What is the M line?
blocks.explanation: The M line is a dark line that may be present at the centre of the H-band of a sarcomere. It helps stabilize the thick filaments.

book_ref.quote: The center of the H-band may have a dark line

blocks.prompt: 67 Name the roles of the three polypeptides of troponin.
blocks.explanation: Troponin, present at regular intervals on thin filaments, has three polypeptides: one is inhibitory and binds to actin; the second binds to tropomyosin to keep it in place; the third binds to calcium ions.

book_ref.quote: One polypeptide is inhibitory and binds to actin

blocks.prompt: 68 State the sliding filament model.
blocks.explanation: The sliding filament model explains how a muscle contracts: a muscle contracts when its thin myofilaments slide past the thick ones so that they overlap to a greater degree.

book_ref.quote: The sliding filament model explains how a muscle contracts.

blocks.prompt: 69 What is the role of acetylcholine in muscle contraction?
blocks.explanation: When a nerve impulse reaches the muscle, the motor neuron releases the neurotransmitter acetylcholine at the synapse. It stimulates the sarcolemma to produce its own electrochemical impulses, which are carried into the fibre to the T-tubules.

book_ref.quote: It stimulates the sarcolemma to produce its own electrochemical impulses

blocks.prompt: 70 What is the role of calcium ions in muscle contraction?
blocks.explanation: The impulse reaches the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which releases calcium ions into the cytosol. Calcium binds to troponin, which shifts tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin, so myosin heads can bind.

book_ref.quote: The SR releases calcium ions into the cytosol.

blocks.prompt: 71 What is a cross-bridge?
blocks.explanation: When the binding sites on actin are exposed, the myosin heads bind to them. This link between a myosin head and actin is a cross-bridge; the bending of the heads then pulls the actin (power stroke).

book_ref.quote: the myosin heads bind to them and form cross-bridges

blocks.prompt: 72 What changes occur in a sarcomere during the power stroke?
blocks.explanation: The sarcomere shortens: Z-lines come closer together and the H-zone disappears. Adjacent A-bands come closer to each other but do not shorten. This occurs in all sarcomeres at once, so the muscle contracts.

book_ref.quote: bringing Z-lines closer together and H-zone disappears

blocks.prompt: 73 What is the role of ATP in separating myosin heads from actin?
blocks.explanation: After the pull, the myosin head receives a new ATP molecule, which lets it detach from actin. Splitting this ATP into ADP and Pi puts the head back into its original conformation, so the cross-bridge cycle can begin again.

book_ref.quote: Splitting of this ATP into ADP and Pi puts the head into its original conformation

blocks.prompt: 74 What is rigor mortis? Why does it occur?
blocks.explanation: Rigor mortis is the muscle stiffness of death. After death cells can no longer produce ATP, so the cross-bridges between myosin heads and actin cannot be broken. A living cell always has enough ATP to let the heads detach.

book_ref.quote: After death, the cells can no longer produce ATP

blocks.prompt: 75 Differentiate between origin and insertion of a muscle.
blocks.explanation: Both are attachment points of a muscle on two different bones.

book_ref.quote: while the end attached to the bone that moves is the insertion

rows: End attached to the bone that stays stationary during contraction
End attached to the bone that moves
Example: hamstrings originate at the pelvic girdle and top of the femur
Example: hamstrings insert at the upper parts of the fibula and tibia

blocks.prompt: 76 Differentiate between flexor and extensor muscles.
blocks.explanation: They form an antagonistic pair at a joint.

book_ref.quote: When the opposing muscle, called extensor, contracts it straightens the bone

rows: Bends the bone at the joint when it contracts
Straightens the bone at the joint when it contracts
Relaxed while the extensor contracts
Relaxed while the flexor contracts
At the knee: hamstrings
At the knee: quadriceps

blocks.prompt: 77 Differentiate between hamstrings and quadriceps.
blocks.explanation: Both are muscle groups of the thigh moving the knee joint.

book_ref.quote: Extension, or straightening, of the lower leg is done by the quadriceps.

rows: A group of three muscles at the back of the thigh
A group of four muscles at the front of the thigh
Flex (bend) the lower leg
Extend (straighten) the lower leg
Origin: pelvic girdle and top of the femur
Origin: ilium (part of pelvic girdle) and femur
Insertion: upper parts of the fibula and tibia
Insertion: patella (kneecap) and tibia

blocks.prompt: 78 What is muscle fatigue? How is it relieved?
blocks.explanation: Muscle fatigue is a decline in muscle performance after prolonged or intense physical activity or due to some disease. It typically improves with rest; if severe, it requires medical attention.

book_ref.quote: Muscle fatigue means a decline in muscle performance

blocks.prompt: 79 Give reason: a muscle stops contracting when its ATP supply is used up.
blocks.explanation: During exercise, muscles use ATP to contract. When the supply of ATP is depleted, the muscle can no longer contract; this is one factor of muscle fatigue.

book_ref.quote: When the supply of ATPs is depleted, the muscle is no longer able to contract.

blocks.prompt: 80 How can muscle cramps be relieved?
blocks.explanation: Gently stretch and massage the affected muscle. Applying heat or cold to the area and using pain-relieving medications can also help.

book_ref.quote: To relieve muscle cramps, gently stretch and massage the affected muscle.

blocks.prompt: 81 What is hypocalcaemia? How is it related to tetany?
blocks.explanation: Hypocalcaemia is a low level of calcium in the blood. It is the most common cause of tetany and may be due to vitamin D deficiency, renal failure or thyroid disorders.

book_ref.quote: which may be due to vitamin D deficiency, renal failure, or thyroid disorders

blocks.prompt: 82 How is tetany caused by salt imbalance treated?
blocks.explanation: Treatment of tetany depends on the underlying cause. If it is caused by salt imbalances, treatment may involve calcium or magnesium supplements or intravenous fluids to restore electrolyte balance.

book_ref.quote: Treatment for tetany depends on the underlying cause.

blocks.prompt: 83 In the rod-and-lever system of the skeleton, what acts as the rod, fulcrum, effort and load?
blocks.explanation: Rods: bones. Fulcrums (pivot points): joints. Effort: muscles. Load: the weight or resistance moved. When a weight is lifted at the elbow, the forearm bones (radius and ulna) are the lever, the elbow is the fulcrum and the biceps gives the effort.

book_ref.quote: Muscles generate the effort or force, while the weight or resistance being moved is the load.
